issues.quote: The regulator on the wall had stopped, and his hand was closed on his watch.
issues.fact: The fact sheet gives no stopped regulator and no watch in the victim's hand. The only clock readings are the kitchen clock and the hall clock strike.
issues.misreading: A solver could treat the stopped regulator and the watch as evidence of the time of death, or read the watch as showing a reading that belongs to the timeline. Neither is in the sheet, so this invents a clock-based clue.

issues.quote: I went up the back stairs to the atelier, and I called to him, and he did not answer. He was on the floor under the long windows.
issues.fact: The sheet says nothing about where the master was found or which route Rosa took to reach him.
issues.misreading: A solver could take the atelier, the back stairs, and the position under the windows as whereabouts facts that narrow who could have been there or when, which the sheet does not support.

issues.quote: After that I went up to fetch the master for the toast.
issues.fact: The sheet gives no time for when Rosa went up, only that the hall clock struck eleven while her kitchen clock showed 11:13.
issues.misreading: A solver could read "after that" as a short, specific interval after the 11:13 reading, or as immediately after the piano stopped, which implies a duration the sheet does not give.

issues.quote: I set it myself, every Sunday, for ten years.
issues.fact: The sheet only says the kitchen clock is kept a quarter of an hour fast on purpose. It gives no setting history or length of service.
issues.misreading: The "every Sunday, for ten years" detail suggests a long-standing, reliable offset, which a solver might use to argue the 15-minute correction was never mistaken. That is an inference the sheet does not state.
